title: Public-entity accessibility discovery before service design
subtitle: A bounded example showing what the source establishes, what it does not, and what to learn next

readerSummary.question: Does an approaching accessibility deadline prove that a new compliance service should be built?
readerSummary.shortAnswer: No. The official deadline is real context, but it does not show which problems buyers still have, how they solve them now, or whether they would pay for a new service.
readerSummary.whyItMatters: Treating a rule as automatic proof of demand can lead to building before the actual problem is understood.
whatIsKnown: The current official page gives different compliance dates according to entity size and type.
whatIsNotKnown: Which accessibility and procurement problems remain poorly served.
Whether the affected organizations would buy a new service rather than use staff or existing providers.
readerSummary.nextStep: Choose one state and one kind of public entity, then learn from buyers, operators, and affected users before designing the service.

concepts.name: A deadline is not the same as buyer demand
concepts.plainMeaning: A rule can require an organization to act by a date. It does not, by itself, tell us what the organization struggles with, what alternatives it has, or whether it will pay a new provider.
concepts.whyItMattersHere: The deadline explains why accessibility work has a time boundary. Separate buyer research is still needed before calling that work a business opportunity.

history.whatChanged: The Department of Justice published the Title II web and mobile-app rule, and the current official page records an April 2026 interim final rule with updated compliance dates.
history.whyItChanged: This example establishes that the official dates changed; it does not claim to have established the policy reasons for the amendment.

whatIsWellEstablished: The official page is an appropriate first-party source for the dates it states.
A compliance date and evidence of willingness to buy answer different questions.
whatIsStillDebated: Which problems are important enough for a selected entity class to fund externally.
Whether internal staff, existing providers, or a new service would be the preferred response.
commonMisunderstandings: A large population affected by a rule is not automatically a large reachable market.
An official source can establish the rule without establishing a buyer's unmet need.
limits: This concept does not determine whether the rule applies to a particular entity.
It does not replace direct research with buyers, operators, or affected users.

researchQuestions.question: What current federal dates govern the scoped entities?
researchQuestions.startingPoint: A deadline appears to create urgency, but the date must be verified before it can even supply context.
researchQuestions.whyItMatters: An obsolete date could create false urgency and distort every later business judgment.
researchQuestions.howItWasNarrowed: The broad question about an accessibility market was split so that the official date could be checked separately from buyer problems and willingness to pay.
whatItDoesNotAnswer: Whether the rule applies to a particular unnamed entity.
Whether any buyer needs a new service.
researchQuestions.decisionItInforms: Prevent an obsolete deadline from driving the opportunity claim.

researchQuestions.question: Which accessibility and procurement jobs remain poorly served?
researchQuestions.startingPoint: Organizations face a rule, but their actual work, obstacles, alternatives, and authority to buy are still unknown.
researchQuestions.whyItMatters: A service is useful only if it improves a real situation for the people doing, buying, or experiencing the work.
researchQuestions.howItWasNarrowed: The question asks about one future state and one entity class so that different roles and procurement paths are not flattened into a national assumption.
whatItDoesNotAnswer: How common any discovered problem is nationally.
Whether a proposed solution will work or make economic sense.
researchQuestions.decisionItInforms: Decide whether any service concept deserves design work.

claims.statement: Select one state and entity class, then run accessible problem and procurement discovery before designing a compliance service.

scope.generalizationBoundary: The recommendation authorizes only the stated research.

confidence.basis: Decision recommendation under decisive missing buyer evidence.

assumptions: Accessible recruitment is feasible at proportionate cost.
exceptions: Stop if ethical, accessibility, or procurement access prerequisites fail.

inferences.reasoning: A current regulatory date supplies context but cannot establish buyer problems. Because that buyer evidence is still missing, a small and reversible discovery study is more justified than building a service.
assumptions: Discovery is cheaper and more reversible than service construction.
exceptions: A binding opportunity-independent reason could prohibit even research.
alternativeExplanations: Entities may solve the job internally or through incumbents.
criticalQuestions: Will recruitment cover relevant size, role, and accessibility differences?

uncertainties.description: The prevalence, severity, and purchase priority of the buyer problem are unknown.
uncertainties.basis: No scoped primary buyer study has run.

alternatives.name: Run one-state, one-class discovery
alternatives.mechanism: Interview and observe scoped buyers, operators, and affected users before selecting a service concept.

alternatives.name: Build an automated compliance product now
alternatives.mechanism: Design around the regulatory date without scoped buyer research.
constraints: Cannot claim that automation alone determines conformance

studyPlans.decisionItInforms: Decide whether a concrete service problem merits solution and economics research.
studyPlans.population: People responsible for accessibility, procurement, operations, and affected use in one selected entity class.
studyPlans.samplingAndRecruitment: Purposefully recruit across entity size, role, and accessibility context; record nonresponse and channel effects.
studyPlans.analysis: Code episodes and alternatives; preserve negative cases and role-specific disagreement.
studyPlans.stoppingRule: Stop when each planned heterogeneity cell has evidence or a documented access failure and new sessions cease changing the decision map.
studyPlans.missingness: Report unreachable roles, entities, and disabled-user contexts as material missing evidence.
studyPlans.ethicsAndPrivacy: Use accessible consent, minimize sensitive data, compensate lived-experience participants, and define retention.
studyPlans.generalizationBoundary: No prevalence estimate or national transfer from purposive discovery.
